items.title: Frost forms by water vapour skipping the liquid state entirely
items.claim: Water vapour in cold air can deposit directly onto a windowpane as ice crystals without ever becoming liquid. The reverse — solid to gas without melting — is called sublimation, and is how freeze-drying works.
items.prompt: Why does water sometimes skip the liquid stage?

options.text: Water bends the laws of phase transitions
At pressures below the triple point (6.1 mbar for water) the liquid phase is not stable — water can only exist as solid or vapour, and transitions go directly between them
Frost forms only from existing ice
Liquid water is too dense for cold air

items.reveal_title: Below the triple point, liquid disappears
items.reveal:
Water's triple point sits at 0.01°C and 6.1 millibar — the only temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist. Below this pressure the liquid phase is unstable; water can only be vapour or ice, and crossing the boundary means sublimation or deposition.

At atmospheric pressure (1013 mbar) water can be liquid between 0 and 100°C, but small pockets of supercooled vapour near a cold surface can deposit straight to solid because the local equilibrium prefers ice over the metastable liquid intermediate.

Freeze-drying exploits this: freeze food, lower the pressure below the triple point, and the ice sublimes away with no melting. The structure is preserved, water is removed, and the result is light, stable food (instant coffee, astronaut meals, pharmaceutical formulations).
items.why: Solid to gas skipping liquid is treated as a curiosity. It is the dominant transition at low pressure and underpins multibillion-dollar industries.

items.title: EDTA can pull rust out of a bridge
items.claim: EDTA is a hexadentate ligand — it wraps around metal ions with six binding sites and stabilises them dramatically against precipitation. Add EDTA to a rusty surface and it pulls iron(III) into solution as a soluble complex.
items.prompt: Why is a chelating ligand so much more effective than six water molecules?

options.text: EDTA forms covalent bonds; water just hydrogen-bonds
Replacing six independent water ligands with one hexadentate EDTA releases six water molecules into bulk solvent — entropy increases dramatically, driving the equilibrium toward the chelate

items.reveal:
Suppose [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + EDTA4- in solution. The product is [Fe(EDTA)]- plus six free water molecules. Even though Fe-O bonds in the EDTA complex are not radically stronger than Fe-O bonds with water, the entropy change is large and positive — one big complex plus six free waters is much more disordered than seven loose particles.

Formation constants for EDTA complexes typically exceed 10 to the 20 — extraordinarily stable.

Applications: EDTA in cleaning products removes iron and calcium stains; in food (E385) it prevents metal-catalysed oxidation; in medicine, it treats lead and mercury poisoning by chelating the toxic metal so the kidneys can excrete it.
items.why: Bond strength is the obvious explanation. Entropy of releasing many small ligands at once is what really stabilises chelates.

items.title: Louis Pasteur separated mirror-image molecules with tweezers
items.claim: In 1848 Louis Pasteur, a 26-year-old chemist, was studying sodium ammonium tartrate crystals from wine. He noticed two distinct mirror-image crystal forms. He separated them by hand with tweezers and showed each rotated polarised light in opposite directions. Chirality was discovered.
items.prompt: What does Pasteur's work imply about biology?

options.text: Living systems prefer one enantiomer over the other — L-amino acids in proteins, D-sugars in DNA. Biological receptors are chiral and distinguish enantiomers like a hand distinguishes left and right gloves

items.reveal_title: A tweezers experiment with deep consequences
items.reveal:
Racemic tartaric acid (a 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers) crystallised in two distinct hemihedral forms. Pasteur, with a hand lens and tweezers, separated the crystals into two piles. Each pile dissolved gave equal and opposite rotations of polarised light. Combined, they cancelled exactly.

The implications were enormous. Carbon atoms with four different groups are chiral; molecules can come in left- and right-handed forms with the same atoms but different spatial arrangements.

Biology is overwhelmingly homochiral. All natural amino acids (except glycine) are L-form; all natural DNA sugars are D-form. Why life chose one hand over the other is still unknown. Some theories invoke parity violation in beta decay, circularly polarised light from neutron stars, or simple chance amplified by autocatalytic prebiotic chemistry.

The thalidomide disaster (1957-1962) drove home that pharmaceutical chirality matters: one enantiomer sedates morning sickness, the other causes severe birth defects.
items.why: A patient observation with hand tools opened a deep window into the molecular geometry of life.
